name: Substitution of the authority of the ancients for the authority of the Church
plain_explanation: Renaissance thinkers still deferred heavily to authority, but shifted from deferring to the Church to deferring to classical antiquity. Because ancient authors disagreed among themselves, this still required individual judgment to decide which authority to follow, making it a genuine step toward intellectual independence -- though most Italians still would not hold an opinion unsupported by either antiquity or the Church.
precise_definition: Russell's account of the Renaissance's partial, transitional emancipation: 'they substituted the authority of the ancients for that of the Church. This was, of course, a step towards emancipation, since the ancients disagreed with each other, and individual judgement was required to decide which of them to follow.'
why_it_mattered: This explains why the Renaissance could break scholasticism's grip without yet producing genuinely independent philosophy -- true intellectual autonomy would only fully emerge with seventeenth-century science.
historical_origin: Develops through the fifteenth century as classical texts and Greek scholarship (via Byzantine contacts) became more widely available.
examples: The Council of Ferrara (1438) debate over Plato's superiority to Aristotle
competing_positions: Full scholastic deference to Church and Aristotelian authority
influence_on_later_thinkers: Prepares the ground for the fuller intellectual independence achieved by seventeenth-century science (Chapter VI).
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly tied to the Church's declining monopoly on intellectual authority.
